title: Lesson 6: Adulting with Purpose
subtitle: Living Independently with Faith, Intention, and Eternal Perspective
primary_source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Weight of Glory' (1941), on the eternal significance of ordinary human actions and relationships
key_concepts: Stewarding your independence for God's glory
An eternal perspective on daily life

verses.text: "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of trouble come and the years approach when you will say, 'I find no pleasure in them.'"
verses.commentary: Solomon's wisdom urges young people to center their lives on God from the very beginning of adulthood — not waiting until old age or crisis. The habits, priorities, and spiritual disciplines you establish now will shape the trajectory of your entire life. Remember your Creator in every decision, relationship, and daily routine.

verses.text: "And whatever you do, whether in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him."
verses.commentary: There is no division between 'sacred' and 'secular' in the Christian life. Paying your bills, cooking dinner, maintaining your car, and showing up to work on time are all acts of worship when done in the name of Jesus. Adulting with purpose means recognizing that every moment is an opportunity to glorify God.

verses.text: "Be very careful, then, how you live — not as unwise but as wise, making the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil."
verses.commentary: Purposeful living requires vigilance and wisdom. The freedom of independent adulthood can be used wisely or squandered. Paul urges believers to 'redeem the time' — to make every day count for eternity by living with intention, discipline, and an awareness of how precious each moment is.

content.heading: Introduction: Freedom with a Purpose
paragraphs: Independent adulthood brings a freedom you have never experienced before. No one tells you when to wake up, what to eat, how to spend your evening, or when to go to bed. This freedom is a gift from God — but like all gifts, it comes with responsibility.

The difference between thriving and merely surviving as an independent adult often comes down to one word: purpose. Living with purpose means making intentional choices about how you spend your time, energy, money, and attention — choices guided not by impulse or peer pressure but by your identity as a child of God and your calling to glorify Him in all things.

content.heading: Building Daily Disciplines
paragraphs: Successful independent living rests on daily disciplines that may seem mundane but are profoundly important. These include maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, preparing nutritious meals, keeping your living space clean and organized, managing your finances regularly, exercising for physical health, and — most importantly — maintaining daily time with God in prayer and Scripture.

Without the structure that parents and school provided, you must create your own. Establish morning and evening routines that anchor your day. Use a calendar or planner to manage commitments. Set reminders for bills, appointments, and maintenance tasks. These habits are not restrictions on your freedom — they are the framework that makes productive, purposeful living possible.

The spiritual disciplines are especially critical during this transition. Daily Bible reading, prayer, church attendance, fellowship with other believers, and service keep you connected to God and grounded in truth during a season of significant change. Do not let the busyness of adult life crowd out the most important relationship you have.

content.heading: Navigating Loneliness and Transition
paragraphs: Moving into independent living often brings unexpected loneliness. You may miss the daily presence of family, the built-in social structure of school, or the familiarity of your hometown. These feelings are normal and do not indicate failure — they indicate that God designed you for community.

Combat loneliness by investing in relationships intentionally. Join a church small group, invite coworkers or neighbors for dinner, maintain long-distance friendships through regular communication, and be willing to initiate rather than waiting for others to reach out. Building community as an adult requires more effort than it did as a student, but the relationships you build are often deeper and more enduring.

Be patient with yourself during transitions. Adjusting to a new city, a new job, or a new living situation takes time. Trust that God is with you in the unfamiliar (Deuteronomy 31:8) and that He is using this season to grow your faith, independence, and character in ways that will bear fruit for years to come.

content.heading: Living with Eternal Perspective
paragraphs: C.S. Lewis wrote that 'there are no ordinary people' — that every human interaction carries eternal significance because every person you encounter is an immortal soul. This perspective transforms daily life from a series of tasks into a sacred calling.

Adulting with purpose means remembering that your life is not your own — you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Your career, your finances, your relationships, your talents, and your time all belong to God. You are a steward, not an owner. This truth is not burdensome but liberating — it means that every faithful act, no matter how small, has eternal value.

As you launch into independent adulthood, go with confidence — not in your own abilities, but in the God who called you, equips you, and walks with you. The same God who has been faithful throughout your life will continue to be faithful in every new chapter. Trust Him, serve Him, and let your life be a testimony to His grace and goodness in a world that desperately needs to see it.

reflection_questions.question: How does Colossians 3:17 transform the way you view ordinary daily tasks like cooking, cleaning, and paying bills? Why is there no true division between 'sacred' and 'secular' in the Christian life?
reflection_questions.guidance: Consider how doing everything 'in the name of the Lord Jesus' changes the meaning and motivation behind mundane responsibilities. Think about how this perspective can combat the feeling that daily adult tasks are meaningless.

reflection_questions.question: What daily disciplines and routines will be most important for you as you transition to independent living? How can you ensure that spiritual disciplines remain a priority?
reflection_questions.guidance: Consider practical strategies for maintaining Bible reading, prayer, church attendance, and fellowship when no one is reminding you. Think about how spiritual health supports every other area of life — emotional, relational, financial, and physical.

reflection_questions.question: C.S. Lewis said there are 'no ordinary people' and that every interaction has eternal significance. How should this perspective shape the way you treat neighbors, coworkers, and strangers in your daily life?
reflection_questions.guidance: Consider how viewing every person as an immortal soul created in God's image changes the way you interact with the cashier, the neighbor, the difficult coworker, and the stranger in need. Think about how small acts of kindness can have eternal ripple effects.
